cards.title: Introduction to Java Packages
cards.content:
A package in Java is a mechanism used to group related classes, interfaces, enumerations, and annotations. Think of it as a folder structure in a directory.

Why use packages?

  • Namespace management: Resolves naming conflicts (e.g., you can have two classes named User in different packages).
  • Access Control: Packages help regulate access to classes and members.
  • Maintainability: Keeps large projects organized and easy to navigate.

cards.title: Declaring a Package
cards.content:
To put a class inside a package, you must declare the package name at the very beginning of your Java file. It must be the first non-comment statement in the file.

package com.developer.utility;

public class Calculator {
    public int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }
}

Note: The directory structure of the source file must match the package structure exactly (e.g., com/developer/utility/Calculator.java).

cards.title: Importing Packages
cards.content:
To use a class from another package, you must use the import statement. You can import a single class, an entire package (using wildcard *), or static members.

// Importing a specific class
import java.util.ArrayList;

// Importing all classes in a package
import java.util.*;

// Importing static members directly
import static java.lang.Math.PI;

Note: The java.lang package is imported automatically by default in every Java application.

cards.title: Packages & Access Control
cards.content:
Java packages are deeply connected to access levels:

  • package-private (default): If no access modifier is declared, members are only visible to classes within the same package.
  • protected: Members are accessible to classes within the same package AND subclasses in different packages.
  • public: Members are visible to classes in all packages.

By default, classes inside the same package have implicit trust and can access each other's default/package-private elements.

cards.title: JAR (Java Archive) Packaging
cards.content:
To distribute your packaged application, you compile it into a ZIP-compressed archive file known as a JAR (Java Archive).

Key properties of JARs:

  • They contain compiled .class files, resources (images, property files), and metadata.
  • The MANIFEST.MF file inside the META-INF/ directory specifies the entry point (the class containing the main method) using the Main-Class attribute.

Example compile & run command:

jar cfm App.jar manifest.txt com/developer/utility/*.class
java -jar App.jar

cards.title: Naming Best Practices
cards.content:
To ensure unique packages worldwide, follow these standard practices:

  • Reverse Domain Name: Use your organization's internet domain reversed as the prefix (e.g., com.google, org.apache).
  • Lowercase letters: Always use lowercase to avoid conflicts with class names.
  • Keyword escape: If your domain contains a Java keyword, prepend an underscore (e.g., com.example.switch should become com.example._switch).

cards.title: Modular Packaging (Java 9+)
cards.content:
Introduced in Java 9, the Java Platform Module System (JPMS) added a higher level of packaging abstraction above standard packages.

A module is defined using a module-info.java file at the root source folder. It declares:

  • Which internal packages are exported (made public) to other modules.
  • Which other modules it requires to work.
module com.academy.app {
    requires java.sql;
    exports com.academy.app.services;
}
